input.new_string:
## Leaving several PRs open after one sweep, subscribe every one of them

An unsubscribed PR gets noticed only on a manual re-poll, while a subscribed one's merge or comment arrives as an activity event the moment it happens. When a run's output is more than one open PR, subscribe all of them before ending the session, not a sample.

## `search_code`'s index can lag — don't trust it alone to enumerate affected repos

Scoping a sweep across many repos by `search_code` alone can silently undercount: its index has been observed to lag well behind a repo's actual content, returning a fraction of the repos a direct check turns up for the identical pattern. Before scoping a fleet-wide sweep on a search result, cross-check against a direct, structural enumeration (fetch each candidate repo's own relevant file rather than relying on the search index to have seen it).

## The rendered PR-diff view can silently omit a new file — confirm with git, not the UI

A GitHub PR's rendered diff view has been observed to drop a new root-level file or directory addition from what it displays, even though the file is genuinely present in the commit. Confirm whether a file landed with `git ls-files` / `git diff --stat` against the branch, never by reading the rendered diff — a false "it's missing" read costs a round-trip and an unnecessary re-push.

# core — working with Claudinite itself

- **Reading a rule, check or skill that arrived from Claudinite** — it is vendored, under
  `.claudinite/shared/`, and the update flows replace that whole tree. Never edit anything there:
  change it in the canon, or carry the difference in this repo's own `.claudinite/local/packs/`.

- **Finding a mounted skill, or following a link from inside one you already loaded** — a canon
  skill lives at `.claudinite/shared/packs/<pack>/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`; there is no flat
  `.claudinite/shared/skills/`. When the `Skill` tool announces a per-session flat "base directory"
  (e.g. `.claude/skills/<name>/`) that holds only that one `SKILL.md`, any relative link the
  skill's own text carries (to a sibling doc, a sibling skill) was written for its real home and
  dangles from that announced base — resolve such links against the canon path instead.

- **Wanting a pack's rules to apply here** — declare its id in `.claudinite-settings.json`. Nothing
  activates by being mounted, fingerprinted or present on disk, so a pack whose files you can see
  but whose id is undeclared contributes no prose, no checks, no skills and no tasks.

- **Adding a pack** — run the `adopt-pack` skill, which declares it, asks its adoption questions,
  re-vendors and scaffolds. Never hand-copy a pack's content into the repo.

- **Setting a project up on Claudinite for the first time** — the `adopt-claudinite` skill.

- **Deciding which pack owns a lesson** — read `packs/directory.GENERATED.md`, the catalog of
  *every* canon pack, never the mounted subset: the mount holds only what this repo declares, so the
  pack that owns the territory may be absent and invisible. When the owning pack is merely too
  narrow, widen its `ruleRoutingGuidance.belongs` rather than opening a local pack beside it.

- **Judging whether Claudinite is current here** — read the stamp's `engineVersion` and
  `packVersions`, never `claudinite.updated` or `ref`: the versioned flows stamp versions and
  nothing else, so those two hold the provenance of the last full re-vendor rather than of this
  mount, and a member converging nightly reads as weeks stale.

- **Answering "why did the mount not update"** — read the member's own artifacts (its declaration,
  its stamp, the head sha's runs) before theorizing about a platform setting; propose a settings
  change as a conclusion, never as a diagnosis.

- **A file a vendored module references but that is absent from `.claudinite/shared/`** — that is
  evidence about the vendor set, not the canon: check the canon itself (a shallow clone, or a
  canon-scoped session) before filing an issue claiming it was never shipped, and where you can't,
  report only that the mount lacks the file.

- **An engine source comment under the mount points at a design doc** (`DESIGN.md`) — the mount
  vendors `.mjs` sources and pack docs only, never the canon's internal design-doc tree, so the
  pointer dangles in every member. Read the module's own header comment, which restates what the
  missing section would have said. (1)

- **Running `check_the_world.mjs` or `check_the_work.mjs` and seeing no output** — that is the
  clean result, not a stall: a run with no findings prints nothing and exits `0`. Append
  `; echo "EXIT:$?"` if in doubt, rather than a second pass of `--help`/`head`/`tail` hunting for
  confirmation that silence is safe. (2)

- **Pushing a change that touches `.github/workflows/`, `.claudinite-checks.json` or pack config**

  push → CI → fix round trip on a finding it reports in seconds:

---
name: unattended-agents
description: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
---

# Agent architecture principles

- An agent invoked **unattended** by automation (a CI workflow, not interactive Claude Code) should be left only the part of the task that genuinely needs its judgment; hard-code every deterministic part — the setup before *and* the wrap-up after — in the workflow around it. A step described in prose is one the agent can skip, reorder, or improvise; a step the workflow runs in code can't be fumbled, and the shorter prompt keeps the agent on the one thing only it can do. Push that boundary continually: each time a step proves mechanical, move it out of the prompt and into the workflow.
- When a routine needs a capability its own runtime lacks — a credential spanning more repos than the session's allowlist, an execution surface the sandbox can't reach — wrap that part as a **dispatch-only executor** (e.g. a `workflow_dispatch`-only GitHub Actions workflow holding the privileged token) that the routine triggers and awaits. The executor carries **no schedule of its own**: give it a cron and it silently becomes a second orchestrator with a competing trigger. One schedule, owned by the orchestrating routine; executors run only when dispatched. State only the executor's *contract* in the routine's prose (what it computes, what the agent may rely on) — its internal rules live in its code, unlike validators of the agent's *own* output, which the prose must still teach (see the routine-folder rules below).
- **The routine's own in-session steps reach GitHub through the session's MCP tools — never a REST client or a `GITHUB_TOKEN`.** This is the corollary of the rule above: the steps a routine runs *itself* operate over the repos the session was granted, which the MCP GitHub tools already cover, so they need no token. A REST client, a raw `api.github.com` `fetch`, or a `process.env.GITHUB_TOKEN` read in in-session code (a migration pass, an agent-stage worker doc's steps) is the tell that the step was mis-built as if it were the CI *executor* — and it will 401 in the MCP-only session it's scheduled in, silently turning the run into a no-op. Only the part that genuinely needs the broader credential moves to a dispatch-only executor; everything else is MCP. *Diagnosing* whether in-session code can reach a host: probe with a tool that honors the sandbox's `HTTPS_PROXY` — `curl` does — never a bare `node -e "fetch(...)"`, whose global `fetch` ignores `HTTPS_PROXY` and goes **direct**, returning a verdict that bypasses (and so misreports) the proxy's real one.
- Size a routine spec at checklist altitude, and re-compress after every scope addition — specs bloat by accretion, not by any one edit. Keep it to terse imperative bullets stating outcomes, bounds, and judgment criteria; a delegated step gets its contract only, procedure another doc owns gets a pointer (never a restatement), and a why-clause earns its place only where the rule is surprising. Symptoms you've absorbed what belongs elsewhere: the spec re-explains a companion script's logic or a sibling doc's steps, or has grown to several times its sibling routines (the house norm is ~40–90 lines).
- Bound an unattended agent's **write surface**, and enforce it from outside the agent. Pre-create the exact file(s) it may edit, tell it to touch nothing else (no new files, no edits to shared code it might be tempted to "improve"), and after it stops, verify the diff in the workflow — reverting anything outside the allowed set rather than trusting the prompt. Prose is a request; the post-hoc diff check is the guarantee, so a misbehaving agent's blast radius is bounded no matter how it strays. Anything the agent would otherwise reach into belongs inlined in its own file (as a source's local helper), not edited in place.
- In a multi-stage unattended pipeline, converge **every** failure exit — including an infrastructure failure in a pre-agent setup stage (a fetch, an auth step, scaffolding) — to the same human-triage state as an agent-detected failure. A setup-phase failure that reports itself but leaves the original trigger untouched (e.g. a label still set) makes the item look unprocessed rather than blocked, silently defeating the escalation path. Treat every failure mode as equivalent from the triage perspective.
- An unattended agent must **never invoke a tool that surfaces a blocking approval it cannot answer** — there is no human present to click "Allow," so the run stalls indefinitely on step one. The multi-agent-orchestration **Workflow tool is the classic trap**: it mandates an interactive opt-in on *every* run (the prompt only disappears under bypass-permissions / headless modes you cannot rely on the scheduler being in), so a routine that fans out through it hangs before doing any work. Fan out with **plain subagent dispatch** (the Agent/Task tool) instead — it carries no such gate and the orchestrator honors any phase barriers itself — and reserve the Workflow tool for interactive sessions where a human can consent. The general rule: an unattended agent's whole tool path must be answer-free.
- **Dispatch a subagent under worktree isolation whenever it may commit.** Without it the child works in the parent's checkout and leaves it wherever it finished — on the child's branch — so the parent's branch-scoped end-of-session checks judge the *child's* commits against the *parent's* transcript and file findings the parent cannot act on. Pass the isolation flag on the dispatch (`isolation: "worktree"`); recovering after the fact means checking the parent back onto its own assigned branch and re-verifying everything.
- **A routine that correctly declines has not failed — converge failures, not declines.** When the item a run was dispatched for genuinely cannot be processed (an unreachable source, a dead link, an empty result), record the reason on that item, mark it for human attention, and exit **zero**. Failing the task instead raises a *second* human-triage signal for the same item and reports the pipeline as broken when it in fact judged correctly. Partial success is the same shape: the items that did process still land.
- **A run that *skips* its work still exits 0 — a job whose success and whose no-op look identical from outside is telling you nothing.** A scheduler ran green nightly while skipping its main stage on a misread config value, the only trace one skip line in a log nobody opens on a green run. Make every skip state what it skipped and why in the run's own visible output, and confirm a routine works by reading a *reason*, not an exit code: a skip is a finding to triage, not a pass. And when the defect lives inside the mechanism that updates itself (a vendored mount its own maintenance job refreshes, a bootstrap that installs its own successor), the ordinary route can't carry the fix — recognise the self-reference and land the repair out of band rather than waiting for the broken updater.
- **The session that designed a judgment stage must not be the one that runs it.** A stage that picks the strongest candidate, ranks a set, or decides what matters has to run in a context that never saw it being built — the designing session knows which candidates it had in mind when it chose the heuristic and will find them again, which is an echo, not judgment. Exercise a freshly-built stage in a subagent whose context starts empty, or leave it to the scheduler. Better, make the clean context **structural rather than remembered**: state it in the task spec as a rule the agent reads every run ("do not load context you were not given — the item's own title, body and discussion are what you have, and they are enough"), so the production path is clean without anyone arranging it.
- **A rejected call whose whole purpose was a fallback must be re-issued before you continue.** Arming a timeout wake-up, a watchdog, or a retry is the one class of call whose rejection changes nothing observable: the error scrolls past mid-turn, the run proceeds believing it holds a safety net it never armed, and the gap surfaces only when the primary path dies and nothing recovers it. Read the result of every guard-arming call, re-issue it on the spot, and never claim to be relying on a backstop you didn't confirm.
- **Nothing you post to a tracker can be edited — resolve every value before the comment goes up.** The GitHub toolsets these runs use offer comment *creation* and no comment-update tool, so a comment that goes out wrong can only be appended to, leaving the wrong value and its correction both standing forever. An agent session also has **no ambient clock**: a timestamp is only true if you read it (one shell call) rather than filling a placeholder you mean to fix later. Same for every PR number, sha and label a comment asserts — resolve, then post.
- **When the outcome your ceiling names is mechanically unavailable, stop short and say so — never substitute a riskier action to close the gap.** A routine told to land work through an auto-merging PR cannot when the repository has auto-merge disabled and its checks will not conclude. The gap looks one command wide, and improvising a merge to close it costs more than the unlanded change does. Where a shared delivery procedure exists (Claudinite's `packs/claudinite-tasks/deliver-pr.md`), the merges it licenses — like the direct merge on a base branch that requires nothing, where the arm is rejected "clean status" by design — are the sanctioned path, not a workaround; anything outside them stays unlanded. An open PR plus a plain statement of what could not be armed and why is a complete, honest result. Re-try the mechanism on each run rather than assuming either state is permanent, and drop the workaround the moment it succeeds.
- **A change-gated routine must exclude its *own* writes from its triggers, or it feeds itself.** A routine that commits to, files issues in, or emits artifacts into the same repos it monitors will re-fire on its own output unless every trigger filters it out: its own maintenance commits must not count as "the project changed" (match them by bot-author / `[skip ci]` / a subject convention and exclude — and keep that matcher current with the wording the routine actually writes, or a near-miss silently reads as real work); its own standing-tracker/issue updates must not count as activity (a tracker rewritten every run always sits inside a fixed lookback window, so it re-triggers forever); its own generated plan/report artifact must not count as a repo change. The tell is a routine that fires every cycle on a fleet that is actually quiet. Treat "the routine's inputs never include the routine's outputs" as an invariant when wiring any change-detection signal.
- When an unattended routine takes an **irreversible or outward-facing action** (closing an issue, deleting a branch, sending a message), the spec must **define the trigger condition concretely and default to the safe path** — not just name the action. A bare "close if done" invites a wrong close on a superficial match; "close *only* when the ask is verifiably true of the target's current state — else comment" cannot. State what counts as the condition and where to verify it, and make the reversible option (leave it, comment, escalate) the default whenever the check is inconclusive.
- A `[Merge Without Review]` security warning on a task's own unattended merge is expected, not a finding to escalate — adjudicate it in one step. description: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.

# Agent architecture principles

A step described in prose is one the agent can skip, reorder, or improvise; a step the workflow runs in code can't be fumbled, and the shorter prompt keeps the agent on the one thing only it can do. Push that boundary continually: each time a step proves mechanical, move it out of the prompt and into the workflow.
- When a routine needs a capability its own runtime lacks — a credential spanning more repos than the session's allowlist, an execution surface the sandbox can't reach — wrap that part as a **dispatch-only executor** (e.g. a `workflow_dispatch`-only GitHub Actions workflow holding the privileged token) that the routine triggers and awaits. The executor carries **no schedule of its own**: give it a cron and it silently becomes a second orchestrator with a competing trigger. One schedule, owned by the orchestrating routine; executors run only when dispatched. State only the executor's *contract* in the routine's prose (what it computes, what the agent may rely on) — its internal rules live in its code, unlike validators of the agent's *own* output, which the prose must still teach (see the routine-folder rules below).
- **The routine's own in-session steps reach GitHub through the session's MCP tools — never a REST client or a `GITHUB_TOKEN`.** This is the corollary of the rule above: the steps a routine runs *itself* operate over the repos the session was granted, which the MCP GitHub tools already cover, so they need no token. A REST client, a raw `api.github.com` `fetch`, or a `process.env.GITHUB_TOKEN` read in in-session code (a migration pass, an agent-stage worker doc's steps) is the tell that the step was mis-built as if it were the CI *executor* — and it will 401 in the MCP-only session it's scheduled in, silently turning the run into a no-op. Only the part that genuinely needs the broader credential moves to a dispatch-only executor; everything else is MCP. *Diagnosing* whether in-session code can reach a host: probe with a tool that honors the sandbox's `HTTPS_PROXY` — `curl` does — never a bare `node -e "fetch(...)"`, whose global `fetch` ignores `HTTPS_PROXY` and goes **direct**, returning a verdict that bypasses (and so misreports) the proxy's real one.
- Size a routine spec at checklist altitude, and re-compress after every scope addition — specs bloat by accretion, not by any one edit. Keep it to terse imperative bullets stating outcomes, bounds, and judgment criteria; a delegated step gets its contract only, procedure another doc owns gets a pointer (never a restatement), and a why-clause earns its place only where the rule is surprising. Symptoms you've absorbed what belongs elsewhere: the spec re-explains a companion script's logic or a sibling doc's steps, or has grown to several times its sibling routines (the house norm is ~40–90 lines).

Pre-create the exact file(s) it may edit, tell it to touch nothing else (no new files, no edits to shared code it might be tempted to "improve"), and after it stops, verify the diff in the workflow — reverting anything outside the allowed set rather than trusting the prompt. Prose is a request; the post-hoc diff check is the guarantee, so a misbehaving agent's blast radius is bounded no matter how it strays. Anything the agent would otherwise reach into belongs inlined in its own file (as a source's local helper), not edited in place.

A setup-phase failure that reports itself but leaves the original trigger untouched (e.g. a label still set) makes the item look unprocessed rather than blocked, silently defeating the escalation path. Before diagnosing such a finding as your own — one naming "the branch" or "the commit", or unreferenced/uncommitted changes — check whether a background agent is still running; if a mid-dispatch finding names a branch other than the one you were assigned, switch back to your own branch to clear it rather than treating the finding as real. Never act *on* the shared checkout while a background agent is live in it — don't amend a commit the subagent already pushed, and don't relay a "fix" built from a misread of its in-flight state; if the checkout-back is itself refused by the permission classifier, that refusal is the tell a live subagent is using the checkout, so leave the branch alone until it finishes.
 - **Once a source is delegated to a background subagent, don't also mine or re-analyze it yourself while waiting.** Your own parallel read computes nothing the subagent won't report, so either wait with no tool call or spend the interim on work no subagent owns. And if you catch a flawed prompt moments after dispatching, send a **follow-up message to that same agent** rather than a fresh dispatch over the identical source — a redispatch runs a full second pass in parallel, at full cost.

# claudinite-canon-curation — authoring and policing the packs on a canon's shelf

## Naming and placing content on the shelf

- **Wanting a rule about what the `packs/` tree may reference** — configure the baseline pack's
  `config.barriers`, extending the mechanism generically if a capability is missing. Never
  standalone segregation-checking code. (12)

- **Naming a new canon pack** — name it for the surface it serves rather than the first feature
  you are building for it.

- **Naming a pack whose subject is a Claudinite feature itself** — the `claudinite-` prefix
  (`claudinite-lifecycle`, `claudinite-dashboard`). `claudinite-growth` is grandfathered.
  (convertible → prose-to-checks) (1)

- **Looking for a skill and not finding it in `.claude/skills/`** — read
  `packs/<pack>/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` out of the tracked tree. Mounting filters on the literal
  declaration, so an unmounted skill says nothing about whether its procedure applies. (2)

- **A canon pack's prose naming another pack by literal path** — check the name resolves inside
  every consumer's vendored tree.


## Pack config and shared logic

- **Choosing a value right for nearly every project** — keep it in the pack's own code: ask
  nothing at adoption, write nothing into member config. Read config as optional; unset means the
  default, never "misconfigured".

- **Wanting a `.claudinite-settings.json` entry's config validated** — a real JSON Schema the file
  points at with `$schema`. Never a coded per-pack validation vocabulary or a `configSchema` type
  system on the manifest. (4)

- **Wanting to share logic between two sibling packs** — never `engine/`, which breaks the
  package-manager model, and never a pack-to-pack dependency, which breaks independence. Prefer
  self-describing data; else duplicate, possibly with a drift guard. (5)

## Pack modules and the engine they load against

- **Adding a module under `packs/`** — keep it import-light, and start work after evaluation
  completes (`check(…).catch(…)`), never in a top-level `await`. Discovery imports every
  `pack.mjs` before activation is consulted, so a CLI entry point re-imports mid-evaluation and
  Node exits 13.


- **A pack that fails to load** — it fails the mount's self-test, the converge refuses to land at
  all, and the member cannot receive the pack version that would have fixed it.

## Writing and keeping checks

- **Adding or changing a check** — update the pack's catalog row, and re-run the suite against
  current `main` before merging: a whole-tree aggregate is judged post-merge, so a branch's own
  green never covers it.

- **Writing a check's `fix` text** — name only remedies matching the enforced severity; sessions
  follow the words, not the `severity` field. An advisory's remedies are act on it or leave it,
  never a config-acceptance escape.


- **Writing a check that reads the session transcript** — screen the harness's plain-text
  pseudo-turns, not only tag-wrapped ones. `humanText` in
  `engine/checks/helpers/session-transcript.mjs` drops an entry starting with `<`, so a marker
  like `[Request interrupted by user for tool use]` reads as the owner's latest comment. (6)

- **Fixturing a check that fires at the Stop hook** — carry an interruption marker beside a real
  owner turn. A false positive there spends a whole cycle on something no edit can clear. (7)

- **A doc reached only by following a link out of `RULES.md` or a check's `doc:` line** — if it is
  a how-to wanted at authoring time, convert it into a skill invocable by description.

- **Moving or renaming a file a check's `doc:` field points at** — grep for and re-verify every
  `doc:` by hand. Nothing opens the field until the check fires, so a stale pointer sits broken
  indefinitely.

- **A check built to catch a thing being missing or misnamed** — don't gate its relevance on the
  single signal it exists to validate, or the failure it catches also silences it. Use two
  independent signals, either sufficient. (8)

- **Finding a check that watches only one of two structurally-identical surfaces** — widen it to
  the sibling in the same change rather than filing it separately. (9)

- **Writing a check that a command is still wired into a script or CI step** — match the
  invocation line, never a step's display label. A plain token grep passes on the label alone
  (`step "Normalizer self-test — some-cmd --flag"`) after the real command line is deleted, so
  strip a labeling helper's quoted argument before searching for a surviving invocation. (13)

- **Writing a check that selects inputs by path pattern** — assert over the real tree that its
  scope is non-empty. A pattern left behind by a layout change matches nothing, reads as live, and
  fixtures spelling the same dead layout keep proving the matching.

- **Naming a directory in a finding, a remedy or a doc pointer** — grep the tree for it before
  shipping.

- **Deciding whether an enforced check still earns its keep** — measure its blocking-firing rate
  against what it buys. A check whose firings are dominated by cases where the agent already did
  the right thing is a demotion candidate (check → prose-only). (10)

## Writing pack prose and skills

- **Writing anything into a pack's `RULES.md` that describes rather than instructs** — how a
  mechanism works, or what the pack's own tasks do — not there, where every session in every
  declaring repo pays for it whether or not it is that session's work. Description belongs in the
  module header and the pack `README.md`; a worker's policy belongs in the `task.md` it loads.

- **A documented multi-step procedure the agent re-derives every run** — mechanize it into a
  script the agent runs once. That pattern, not the doc's polish, is the signal.

# core — working with Claudinite itself

- **Reading a rule, check or skill that arrived from Claudinite** — it is vendored, under
  `.claudinite/shared/`, and the update flows replace that whole tree. Never edit anything there:
  change it in the canon, or carry the difference in this repo's own `.claudinite/local/packs/`.

- **Finding a mounted skill, or following a link from inside one you already loaded** — a canon
  skill lives at `.claudinite/shared/packs/<pack>/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`; there is no flat
  `.claudinite/shared/skills/`. When the `Skill` tool announces a per-session flat "base directory"
  (e.g. `.claude/skills/<name>/`) that holds only that one `SKILL.md`, any relative link the
  skill's own text carries (to a sibling doc, a sibling skill) was written for its real home and
  dangles from that announced base — resolve such links against the canon path instead.

- **Wanting a pack's rules to apply here** — declare its id in `.claudinite-settings.json`. Nothing
  activates by being mounted, fingerprinted or present on disk, so a pack whose files you can see
  but whose id is undeclared contributes no prose, no checks, no skills and no tasks.

- **Adding a pack** — run the `adopt-pack` skill, which declares it, asks its adoption questions,
  re-vendors and scaffolds. Never hand-copy a pack's content into the repo.

- **Setting a project up on Claudinite for the first time** — the `adopt-claudinite` skill.

- **Deciding which pack owns a lesson** — read `packs/directory.GENERATED.md`, the catalog of
  *every* canon pack, never the mounted subset: the mount holds only what this repo declares, so the
  pack that owns the territory may be absent and invisible. When the owning pack is merely too
  narrow, widen its `ruleRoutingGuidance.belongs` rather than opening a local pack beside it.

- **Judging whether Claudinite is current here** — read the stamp's `engineVersion` and
  `packVersions`, never `claudinite.updated` or `ref`: the versioned flows stamp versions and
  nothing else, so those two hold the provenance of the last full re-vendor rather than of this
  mount, and a member converging nightly reads as weeks stale.

- **Answering "why did the mount not update"** — read the member's own artifacts (its declaration,
  its stamp, the head sha's runs) before theorizing about a platform setting; propose a settings
  change as a conclusion, never as a diagnosis.

- **A file a vendored module references but that is absent from `.claudinite/shared/`** — that is
  evidence about the vendor set, not the canon: check the canon itself (a shallow clone, or a
  canon-scoped session) before filing an issue claiming it was never shipped, and where you can't,
  report only that the mount lacks the file.

- **An engine source comment under the mount points at a design doc** (`DESIGN.md`) — the mount
  vendors `.mjs` sources and pack docs only, never the canon's internal design-doc tree, so the
  pointer dangles in every member. Read the module's own header comment, which restates what the
  missing section would have said. (1)

- **Running `check_the_world.mjs` or `check_the_work.mjs` and seeing no output** — that is the
  clean result, not a stall: a run with no findings prints nothing and exits `0`. Append
  `; echo "EXIT:$?"` if in doubt, rather than a second pass of `--help`/`head`/`tail` hunting for
  confirmation that silence is safe. (2)

- **A green `check_the_world.mjs` is not evidence the Stop hook will stay quiet** — the two runners
  cover disjoint rule scopes, not the same rules on different triggers: the world runner only sees
  `scope !== 'work'` rules and is wired to CI, while the Stop hook runs `check_the_work.mjs`
  against the diff-plus-transcript `scope: 'work'` rules. Verify "will Stop block me" with
  `check_the_work.mjs`, never by declaring the world runner clean.

- **Pushing a change that touches `.github/workflows/`, `.claudinite-checks.json` or pack config**
  — the world sweep runs in CI, not the Stop hook, so run it locally first rather than spend a
  push → CI → fix round trip on a finding it reports in seconds:

  ```
  node .claudinite/shared/engine/checks/check_the_world.mjs
  ```

Promote the validated survivors of four growth-promote PRs (#1828)

* Promote the validated survivors of four growth-promote PRs

#1715, #1690, #1419 and #1303 sat open for up to two weeks, all conflicting
on version-bump bookkeeping their own pack rules say a promotion should not
write. Rather than rebase four branches, this re-derives the batch against
current main: every candidate rule was re-probed or dropped, and every
duplicate was cut.

Nine of the 27 candidates were already in main, mostly as checks landed by
the prose-to-checks lane since these branches were written:
github-list-without-fields, codeload-tarball-fetch, node/btoa-atob-on-text,
issue-labels-overwrite, pull-request-head-unqualified, the bisection-midpoint
vector in writing-tests, the node module-resolution rule (main's is stronger,
naming ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND and NODE_PATH), and two cloudflare rules the
merged pack already carries. Grepping for each PR's own wording missed three
of these; reading the destination files found them.

Landing, each probed in this session:

- basics: taking over a retiring repo's role; a blocked primary source about
  a real person; the shared-constants rule extended to cross-language pairing
  by name.
- claudinite-canon-curation: check the invocation line, not a step's display
  label — reproduced, a token grep answers 1 while the command runs 0 times.
- claudinite-lifecycle: an engine comment citing a design doc dangles in
  every member (read from compute-vendor-set.mjs); a silent check run is the
  clean result (0 bytes, exit 0).
- git-github-advanced: stop re-searching for a PR template once a repo is
  known templateless — this repo carries none.
- claudinite-growth: the task-worker-restores-main check and its test.
- node: the test-discovery-resolves check and its tests.

Both checks are dated since 2026-09-06 so their advisory grace runs from
when they actually reach members, not from their branches' dates. The node
test file is appended to rather than taken from #1303, whose copy predates
and would have deleted main's btoa/atob coverage.

Nine further candidates make claims about external platforms this sandbox
cannot reach (Firebase and Cloudflare docs unreachable, Apple's JS-rendered)
or about harness behaviour that cannot be forced. They are held back rather
than asserted unverified.

* Prove the two new checks against a consumer, and see them fail

Both checks land blocking, which consumer-safe-change is right to stop: a
severity a member did not ask for turns it red overnight, and canon CI
cannot see a consumer.

Adds two rehearsal shapes, since both checks are additive rather than
renaming or requiring anything:

- growth-member gains a local task worker.sh in the shape
  task-worker-restores-main scans, correctly restoring main before it writes.
- node-consumer is new: a member declaring node whose package.json test
  script names a glob that resolves to a tracked file.

Both converge green with the rules riding their mounts.

Also records the see-it-fail both checks were missing. Neither had been
watched failing — only passing, which the writing-tests skill says proves
nothing for a guard asserting silence:

- weakening task-worker-restores-main's RESTORES pattern to match anything
  turned 3 of its 6 tests red, the inert-on-a-non-worker case included.
- making test-discovery-resolves' resolvesToFiles always return true turned
  3 of node's 14 red, both flagging cases and the resolver's own unit test.

Both restored from HEAD and re-run green.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01BoS871F1tGdzWCiGrTYDeu

* Drop the retiring-role rule, and split four rules that carried two acts

The retiring-role rule is removed on the owner's call: it reads as a
git-github concern rather than working discipline, and its point was thin.
Nothing else cited it and it carried no references entry.

The rest is the prose ration applied to basics/RULES.md, where a rule is one
situation with one trigger. Four rules each carried two, and a reader could
arrive at the second half without the first:

- Referring to a value from more than one place had grown to 163 words
  across four acts — prefer a shared constant, write the guard, keep the
  literal unbroken, and (my own addition last commit) pair cross-language
  copies by name. Now three rules: the choice, writing the guard, and the
  two-language case.
- Deferring a warning you can't fix now bundled filing the issue with
  finding the issue someone already filed. Searching by the finding's
  invariant identifier is its own act, reached without the first.
- Filing anything into the ad-hoc queue bundled the reachability gate with
  what to do when the work is out of reach.

No clause was dropped in any split, and every title survives, so the
append-only guard stays silent. README rows recounted from the repo's own
counter rather than by hand.

{"number":1661,"title":"Promote lessons from EdFringeNow, GCEC, TLDR and Shepherd's local packs","body":"Growth-promote run over the members named in #1657's Context: missingbulb/ClaudiniteWebsite, EdFringeNow, GoogleCalendarEventCreator, LaughCounter, Shepherd, TLDR, WIP.

Read each member's local packs (`.claudinite/local/packs/**/RULES.md`), generalized the candidates, deduped against the whole corpus, and routed the survivors to their owning docs. Most candidates were rejected as either already-covered (several members had independently rediscovered rules already in `basics`, `html`, or the existing `git-github-advanced`/`unattended-agents` docs) or tied to a Claudinite mechanism that has since been redesigned (the retired `resolve-dispatch`/`converge-item.mjs` credential failures several members recorded no longer apply to the current queue model). What's left is genuinely new and portable:

- **`git-github-advanced`**: a workflow's overall conclusion can hide a skipped downstream job (from TLDR's Chrome Web Store release triage); `list_pull_requests`'s `head` filter needs an owner-qualified branch and its `merged` field can't be trusted (from EdFringeNow and Shepherd, independently); `issue_read`'s `get_*` methods reject a PR number (from TLDR).
- **`node`**: a throwaway script that imports a project dependency can't resolve it from an external scratchpad — Node's module resolution never reaches the project's `node_modules` (from GoogleCalendarEventCreator).
- **`claudinite-growth`/`unattended-agents`**: a dispatched subagent's "completed" notification means its turn ended, not that its task is done (from EdFringeNow and Shepherd, independently); and having said you'll wait for a subagent, actually wait rather than redoing its in-flight work yourself (same two repos, independently).

Each touched pack's `version` is bumped and gets a `VERSIONS.md` row. `packs/node/README.md`'s rule index is updated for the new bullet (word count computed via `engine-tests/rule-index.mjs`). Full suite green (`node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')`, 3157/3157).

Refs #1657

# claudinite-canon-curation — authoring and policing the packs on a canon's shelf

## Naming and placing content on the shelf

- **Wanting a rule about what the `packs/` tree may reference** — configure the baseline pack's
  `config.barriers`, extending the mechanism generically if a capability is missing. Never
  standalone segregation-checking code. (12)

- **Naming a new canon pack** — name it for the surface it serves rather than the first feature
  you are building for it.

- **Naming a pack whose subject is a Claudinite feature itself** — the `claudinite-` prefix
  (`claudinite-lifecycle`, `claudinite-dashboard`). `claudinite-growth` is grandfathered.
  (convertible → prose-to-checks) (1)

- **Looking for a skill and not finding it in `.claude/skills/`** — read
  `packs/<pack>/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` out of the tracked tree. Mounting filters on the literal
  declaration, so an unmounted skill says nothing about whether its procedure applies. (2)

- **A canon pack's prose naming another pack by literal path** — check the name resolves inside
  every consumer's vendored tree.


## Pack config and shared logic

- **Choosing a value right for nearly every project** — keep it in the pack's own code: ask
  nothing at adoption, write nothing into member config. Read config as optional; unset means the
  default, never "misconfigured".

- **Wanting a `.claudinite-settings.json` entry's config validated** — a real JSON Schema the file
  points at with `$schema`. Never a coded per-pack validation vocabulary or a `configSchema` type
  system on the manifest. (4)

- **Wanting to share logic between two sibling packs** — never `engine/`, which breaks the
  package-manager model, and never a pack-to-pack dependency, which breaks independence. Prefer
  self-describing data; else duplicate, possibly with a drift guard. (5)

## Pack modules and the engine they load against

- **Adding a module under `packs/`** — keep it import-light, and start work after evaluation
  completes (`check(…).catch(…)`), never in a top-level `await`. Discovery imports every
  `pack.mjs` before activation is consulted, so a CLI entry point re-imports mid-evaluation and
  Node exits 13.


- **A pack that fails to load** — it fails the mount's self-test, the converge refuses to land at
  all, and the member cannot receive the pack version that would have fixed it.

## Writing and keeping checks

- **Adding or changing a check** — update the pack's catalog row, and re-run the suite against
  current `main` before merging: a whole-tree aggregate is judged post-merge, so a branch's own
  green never covers it.

- **Writing a check's `fix` text** — name only remedies matching the enforced severity; sessions
  follow the words, not the `severity` field. An advisory's remedies are act on it or leave it,
  never a config-acceptance escape.


- **Writing a check that reads the session transcript** — screen the harness's plain-text
  pseudo-turns, not only tag-wrapped ones. `humanText` in
  `engine/checks/helpers/session-transcript.mjs` drops an entry starting with `<`, so a marker
  like `[Request interrupted by user for tool use]` reads as the owner's latest comment. (6)

- **Fixturing a check that fires at the Stop hook** — carry an interruption marker beside a real
  owner turn. A false positive there spends a whole cycle on something no edit can clear. (7)

- **A doc reached only by following a link out of `RULES.md` or a check's `doc:` line** — if it is
  a how-to wanted at authoring time, convert it into a skill invocable by description.

- **Moving or renaming a file a check's `doc:` field points at** — grep for and re-verify every
  `doc:` by hand. Nothing opens the field until the check fires, so a stale pointer sits broken
  indefinitely.

- **A check built to catch a thing being missing or misnamed** — don't gate its relevance on the
  single signal it exists to validate, or the failure it catches also silences it. Use two
  independent signals, either sufficient. (8)

- **Finding a check that watches only one of two structurally-identical surfaces** — widen it to
  the sibling in the same change rather than filing it separately. (9)

- **Writing a text/regex-matching check** — the placement convention that makes a lesson findable
  (a gotcha comment sitting right beside the code it applies to) is exactly what makes a comment
  *documenting* the banned pattern land closest to the pattern itself — a plain token match then
  fires on the explanatory comment as readily as on a real offense. Gate on real syntax (a call
  site, an import, a non-comment token) rather than a bare substring, or exclude comment lines
  explicitly.

- **Writing a check that a command is still wired into a script or CI step** — match the
  invocation line, never a step's display label. A plain token grep passes on the label alone
  (`step "Normalizer self-test — some-cmd --flag"`) after the real command line is deleted, so
  strip a labeling helper's quoted argument before searching for a surviving invocation. (13)

- **Writing a check that selects inputs by path pattern** — assert over the real tree that its
  scope is non-empty. A pattern left behind by a layout change matches nothing, reads as live, and
  fixtures spelling the same dead layout keep proving the matching.

- **Naming a directory in a finding, a remedy or a doc pointer** — grep the tree for it before
  shipping.

- **Deciding whether an enforced check still earns its keep** — measure its blocking-firing rate
  against what it buys. A check whose firings are dominated by cases where the agent already did
  the right thing is a demotion candidate (check → prose-only). (10)

## Writing pack prose and skills

- **Writing anything into a pack's `RULES.md` that describes rather than instructs** — how a
  mechanism works, or what the pack's own tasks do — not there, where every session in every
  declaring repo pays for it whether or not it is that session's work. Description belongs in the
  module header and the pack `README.md`; a worker's policy belongs in the `task.md` it loads.

- **A documented multi-step procedure the agent re-derives every run** — mechanize it into a
  script the agent runs once. That pattern, not the doc's polish, is the signal.

diff --git a/packs/claudinite-growth/skills/unattended-agents/SKILL.md b/packs/claudinite-growth/skills/unattended-agents/SKILL.md
index 46c095f..005ec94 100644
--- a/packs/claudinite-growth/skills/unattended-agents/SKILL.md
+++ b/packs/claudinite-growth/skills/unattended-agents/SKILL.md
@@ -21,6 +21,7 @@ description: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agent
 - **When the outcome your ceiling names is mechanically unavailable, stop short and say so — never substitute a riskier action to close the gap.** A routine told to land work through an auto-merging PR cannot when the repository has auto-merge disabled and its checks will not conclude. The gap looks one command wide, and improvising a merge to close it costs more than the unlanded change does. Where a shared delivery procedure exists (Claudinite's `packs/claudinite-tasks/deliver-pr.md`), the merges it licenses — like the direct merge on a base branch that requires nothing, where the arm is rejected "clean status" by design — are the sanctioned path, not a workaround; anything outside them stays unlanded. An open PR plus a plain statement of what could not be armed and why is a complete, honest result. Re-try the mechanism on each run rather than assuming either state is permanent, and drop the workaround the moment it succeeds.
 - **A change-gated routine must exclude its *own* writes from its triggers, or it feeds itself.** A routine that commits to, files issues in, or emits artifacts into the same repos it monitors will re-fire on its own output unless every trigger filters it out: its own maintenance commits must not count as "the project changed" (match them by bot-author / `[skip ci]` / a subject convention and exclude — and keep that matcher current with the wording the routine actually writes, or a near-miss silently reads as real work); its own standing-tracker/issue updates must not count as activity (a tracker rewritten every run always sits inside a fixed lookback window, so it re-triggers forever); its own generated plan/report artifact must not count as a repo change. The tell is a routine that fires every cycle on a fleet that is actually quiet. Treat "the routine's inputs never include the routine's outputs" as an invariant when wiring any change-detection signal.
 - When an unattended routine takes an **irreversible or outward-facing action** (closing an issue, deleting a branch, sending a message), the spec must **define the trigger condition concretely and default to the safe path** — not just name the action. A bare "close if done" invites a wrong close on a superficial match; "close *only* when the ask is verifiably true of the target's current state — else comment" cannot. State what counts as the condition and where to verify it, and make the reversible option (leave it, comment, escalate) the default whenever the check is inconclusive.
+- **Before firing an interactive question, check whether the answer is already decided.** A rule already loaded in context, repo or fleet state one read away (a sibling's config, a pending item's own fields), or the option a picker would mark "(Recommended)" simply being the status quo — any of these settles it without asking. And when a genuine decision remains, batch every open one the run will need into a single question rather than a serial round of asks: each round-trip is pure idle wall time on the human side, and most of what gets asked serially turns out to have been answerable from state already in hand.
 - A `[Merge Without Review]` security warning on a task's own unattended merge is expected, not a finding to escalate — adjudicate it in one step. When a task's declared delivery policy is auto-merge and its target's checks require no human approval (or the arm is rejected `clean status` and a direct merge is the sanctioned path), the harness still flags the completion with a security warning because no human approval appears in the transcript — that is the harness reporting the *shape* of the action, not evaluating whether it was licensed. Confirm the task's declared delivery policy and its outcome ceiling permit the merge, then converge normally; escalating every occurrence to human review would wedge a routine that is designed to merge unattended.
 - A background subagent dispatch shares the parent's working directory unless isolated, so the parent's own end-of-session checks can misread the subagent's activity as its own. Without `isolation: "worktree"`, a background agent runs in the *same* checkout as the session that spawned it, so while it's running: its uncommitted WIP can look like the parent's own dirty diff to a git-status-based finding, and if it switches branches (e.g. checking out another branch to inspect or fix it), a check that reads the current branch now reads *its* branch, not the parent's. Before diagnosing such a finding as your own — one naming "the branch" or "the commit", or unreferenced/uncommitted changes — check whether a background agent is still running; if a mid-dispatch finding names a branch other than the one you were assigned, switch back to your own branch to clear it rather than treating the finding as real. Never act *on* the shared checkout while a background agent is live in it — don't amend a commit the subagent already pushed, and don't relay a "fix" built from a misread of its in-flight state; if the checkout-back is itself refused by the permission classifier, that refusal is the tell a live subagent is using the checkout, so leave the branch alone until it finishes.
 - **Once a source is delegated to a background subagent, don't also mine or re-analyze it yourself while waiting.** Your own parallel read computes nothing the subagent won't report, so either wait with no tool call or spend the interim on work no subagent owns. And if you catch a flawed prompt moments after dispatching, send a **follow-up message to that same agent** rather than a fresh dispatch over the identical source — a redispatch runs a full second pass in parallel, at full cost.

+
+A GitHub PR's rendered diff view has been observed to drop a new root-level file or directory addition from what it displays, even though the file is genuinely present in the commit. Confirm whether a file landed with `git ls-files` / `git diff --stat` against the branch, never by reading the rendered diff — a false "it's missing" read costs a round-trip and an unnecessary re-push.
+
 ## A deleted workflow's old runs outlive it, and no session tool can clear them
 
 Removing a `.yml` from every branch does not remove its run history — the workflow stays listed in
@@ -217,6 +229,7 @@ A list or search API call that isn't bounded returns a full page of full-bodied
 - **Trim the fields, not just the page size.** The per-object field set is what governs the payload, so capping the page can leave the response byte-identical — measured, the same call at two page sizes returned output identical to the character. Ask for the fields you need (`["number","title","state"]` covers most lookups); dropping the body alone is usually the whole difference. Where a tool offers no field selection, narrow the query instead, or take the overflow as the answer and read the spilled result file directly rather than retrying it smaller.
 - **Pass a small explicit page size.** Default page sizes are tuned for a browser, not a tool result; when the answer wanted is one issue or one run, ask for 5–10, never a bare unpaged call.
 - **`actions_list`'s `list_workflow_runs` can ignore `per_page` entirely.** On a repo with enough run history, shrinking the page size — even to 1–3 — returned a byte-identical response, confirmed on two separate repos. Don't retry it smaller: scope the query to a specific run id or one head SHA instead, or read the spilled overflow file directly.
+- **The spilled overflow file for a search call is GitHub's own response envelope** — `{ total_count, incomplete_results, items: [...] }` — not a bare list. Index `['items']` on the first parse instead of guessing the shape across several failed attempts.
 
 All of them, not one: a qualified query still returns a full page, a small page of unqualified matches is still the wrong records, and a small page of full-bodied records still overruns the cap.

git commit -m "$(cat <<'EOF'
Promote 6 portable lessons from CrosswordChat, GCEC, LaughCounter, MissingBulbWebsite, Shepherd

Read the local packs of the six members named in #1861's Context
(CrosswordChat, GoogleCalendarEventCreator, hitbut, LaughCounter,
MissingBulbWebsite, Shepherd). hitbut and CrosswordChat's local packs carry
no portable candidates — hitbut's is an empty placeholder, and
CrosswordChat's is scoped entirely to its own host-page selectors and
calibrated timings.

Most candidates from the other four were already covered: the
GitHub-MCP-overflow (fields/per_page), git-checkout-onto-another-branch,
high-watermark-baseline-reanchoring, subscribe-every-open-PR,
list_pull_requests-merged-field, ToolSearch-fixed-roster, and several
subagent-dispatch rules were independently rediscovered but already live in
basics, git-github-advanced, or unattended-agents. A few referred to a
Claudinite mechanism already fixed since (converge-item.mjs's --repo/
--item-file), and one (a check's own explanatory comment self-matching) is
already solved generically by writing-repo-scanning-checks' stripComments
primitive (issue #201).

What's left is genuinely new and non-duplicate:

- git-github-advanced: list_pull_requests's head filter silently returns
  the wrong PR on a bare branch name (Shepherd, EdFringeNow's sibling
  finding independently); search_code's index can lag well behind a repo's
  real content for a fleet-wide sweep (Shepherd); the rendered PR-diff view
  can drop a new root-level file from its display (Shepherd); the spilled
  overflow file's shape is GitHub's {total_count, incomplete_results,
  items} envelope (Shepherd).
- claudinite-lifecycle: check_the_world.mjs and check_the_work.mjs cover
  disjoint rule scopes, so a green world run is not evidence the Stop hook
  will stay quiet (MissingBulbWebsite, #208's incident).
- claudinite-growth/unattended-agents: check whether an AskUserQuestion's
  answer is already decided (a loaded rule, a one-read-away state, the
  recommended option being the status quo) before firing it, and batch
  every open decision into one question (Shepherd, four measured sessions).

No pack version bumped and no VERSIONS.md row written — pack-version-bump's
job once this lands.

input.body:
Growth-promote run over the members named in #1861's Context: CrosswordChat, GoogleCalendarEventCreator, hitbut, LaughCounter, MissingBulbWebsite, Shepherd.

Read each member's local packs (`.claudinite/local/packs/**/RULES.md` and their own check modules), generalized the candidates, and deduped against the whole corpus (not just the file expected to own each one). hitbut's local pack carries no content beyond its placeholder text, and CrosswordChat's is scoped entirely to its own host-page selectors and calibrated timings for one site — neither had a portable candidate.

Most candidates from the other four repos were already covered: the GitHub-MCP-list-overflow rules (`fields`/`per_page`, the `search_issues` full-text trap), `git checkout <old-branch> -- <paths>` onto another branch, high-watermark baseline re-anchoring, subscribing every open PR, `list_pull_requests`'s untrustworthy `merged` field, the ToolSearch fixed-roster exception, and several subagent-dispatch rules (scratchpad filename collisions, resume-not-redispatch, "completed" ≠ done) were independently rediscovered but already live in `basics`, `git-github-advanced`, or `unattended-agents`. A couple referred to a Claudinite mechanism already fixed since (`converge-item.mjs` now taking `--repo`/`--item-file`). One — a check's own explanatory comment tripping its own text match — is already solved generically by `writing-repo-scanning-checks`'s `stripComments` primitive (#201); I drafted a prose addition for this, found the existing coverage on a second dedup pass, and reverted it.

What's left is genuinely new and non-duplicate:

- **`git-github-advanced`**: `list_pull_requests`'s `head` filter silently returns the wrong PR on a bare branch name (Shepherd); `search_code`'s index can lag well behind a repo's real content, so a fleet-wide sweep needs a direct cross-check (Shepherd); the rendered PR-diff view can drop a new root-level file from its display (Shepherd); the spilled overflow file's shape is GitHub's `{total_count, incomplete_results, items}` envelope (Shepherd).
- **`claudinite-lifecycle`**: `check_the_world.mjs` and `check_the_work.mjs` cover disjoint rule scopes, so a green world run is not evidence the Stop hook will stay quiet (MissingBulbWebsite, from its own #208 incident).
- **`claudinite-growth`/`unattended-agents`**: check whether an `AskUserQuestion`'s answer is already decided (a loaded rule, a one-read-away repo state, the recommended option being the status quo) before firing it, and batch every open decision into one question rather than a serial round (Shepherd, four measured sessions).

No pack `version` bumped and no `VERSIONS.md` row written — `pack-version-bump`'s job once this lands.

`check_the_world.mjs`: 0 blocking, same advisory count as `main` (no new findings). `check_the_work.mjs`: clean.
